question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

LUGUBRIOUS
option_1: Cheerful
option_2: Jovial
option_3: Mournful
option_4: Blithe
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Mournful.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lugubrious (adjective) means looking or sounding sad and dismal, often to an exaggerated degree. (शोकपूर्ण, उदास)
◦ Example: He delivered the news in a lugubrious tone that made matters seem worse than they were.

 

• Mournful carries the same sense — expressing grief or sorrow. (शोकाकुल, विषादपूर्ण)
◦ Example: A mournful silence settled over the gathering.

 

• The word comes from Latin lugere, 'to mourn'. Note that lugubrious usually carries a hint of overdone or theatrical gloom.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Cheerful (प्रसन्न): noticeably happy and optimistic — an antonym.

 

• Option 2: Jovial (हँसमुख, मिलनसार): cheerful and friendly — an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Blithe (निश्चिंत, प्रफुल्लित): casually cheerful and carefree — an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of lugubrious: doleful, dolorous, funereal, morose, sombre.

 

• Do not confuse it with lubricious, an unrelated word of very different meaning; the two are sometimes mixed up because of their similar shape.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

EXTIRPATE
option_1: Eradicate
option_2: Nurture
option_3: Foster
option_4: Implant
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Eradicate.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Extirpate (verb) means to destroy or remove something completely, so that it cannot grow again. (जड़ से उखाड़ना, समूल नष्ट करना)
◦ Example: The campaign aimed to extirpate the weed before it spread to the neighbouring fields.

 

• Eradicate means exactly this — to root out; to wipe out entirely. (उन्मूलन करना)
◦ Example: Smallpox was eradicated by a worldwide vaccination programme.

 

• Both words carry the image of roots: extirpate is from Latin stirps ('a stem or root') and eradicate from radix ('a root').

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Nurture (पोषण करना): to care for and encourage growth — an antonym.

 

• Option 3: Foster (बढ़ावा देना): to promote the development of something — an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Implant (रोपना, स्थापित करना): to fix or plant something firmly — an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of extirpate: exterminate, annihilate, abolish, obliterate, uproot.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

CANDID
option_1: Frank
option_2: Straightforward
option_3: Forthright
option_4: Evasive
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Evasive.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Candid (adjective) means truthful and straightforward, saying openly what one thinks even when it is unwelcome. (स्पष्टवादी, निष्कपट)
◦ Example: In a candid interview she admitted that the project had been mismanaged.

 

• Its opposite is evasive — avoiding a direct answer; deliberately vague. (टालमटोल करने वाला, गोलमोल)
◦ Example: His evasive replies convinced the committee that something was being concealed.

 

• Options 1, 2 and 3 all mean open and direct, so they are synonyms of the given word and may be eliminated as a group.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Frank (खुले दिल का, स्पष्ट): open and unreserved in speech — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Straightforward (सीधा-सादा, स्पष्ट): honest and free from evasion — a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Forthright (मुँहफट, निःसंकोच): direct and outspoken — a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of candid: guarded, secretive, devious, disingenuous, equivocal.

 

• The word also means unposed when used of a photograph — *a candid shot taken without the subject's knowledge*.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To beard the lion in his den
option_1: To take a foolish risk for no good reason
option_2: To confront a formidable opponent on his own ground
option_3: To grow arrogant after an easy success
option_4: To hide quietly from an approaching danger
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To confront a formidable opponent on his own ground.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'To beard the lion in his den' means to go boldly to a powerful or dangerous person and challenge him where he is strongest. (शेर की माँद में जाकर उसे ललकारना; सीधे भिड़ जाना)
◦ Example: He bearded the lion in his den by raising the objection at the chairman's own meeting.

 

• Here beard is a verb meaning 'to confront boldly', from the old gesture of seizing an opponent by the beard. The phrase therefore has nothing to do with facial hair as such.

 

• Two elements are essential: the opponent is formidable, and the confrontation takes place on his ground rather than on neutral territory.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 makes the act merely reckless and leaves out the opponent's own ground; the idiom implies courage, not folly.

 

• Option 3 describes arrogance after success, for which the idiom would be 'to get too big for one's boots'.

 

• Option 4 reverses the sense entirely.

 

NOTE

 

• Related idioms of bold confrontation: to take the bull by the horns, to face the music, to call somebody's bluff, to bell the cat.

question: Choose the correct spelling of a word meaning 'to provide lodging or enough space for'.
option_1: Accommodate
option_2: Accomodate
option_3: Acommodate
option_4: Accommadate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Accommodate.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Accommodate (verb) means to provide lodging or room for; to make space or allowance for. (ठहराना, समायोजित करना)
◦ Example: The new hall can accommodate eight hundred candidates at a time.

 

• The whole difficulty lies in the double letters: the word has two c's and two m's — ac-com-mo-date. It is one of the most frequently misspelt words in English precisely because writers double one pair and not the other.

 

• A useful memory aid: the word is large enough to accommodate two c's and two m's.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Accomodate — wrong; the m has not been doubled.

 

• Option 3: Acommodate — wrong; the c has not been doubled.

 

• Option 4: Accommadate — wrong; the vowel of the third syllable is o, not a (ac-com-mo-date, never -ma-).

 

NOTE

 

• The noun is accommodation, spelt with the same two pairs. Other double-letter traps of the same family: occurrence, embarrass, harass (one r), committee, necessary (one c, two s's), millennium.

question: Find the correctly spelled word meaning 'guided by a sense of duty and careful to do what is right'.
option_1: Conscienteous
option_2: Consciencious
option_3: Conscentious
option_4: Conscientious
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Conscientious.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Conscientious (adjective) means taking care to do one's work thoroughly and to act rightly. (कर्तव्यनिष्ठ, ईमानदार)
◦ Example: She was a conscientious officer who verified every entry herself.

 

• The spelling is best remembered by building it on conscience: CONSCIENCE minus the final -ce, plus -tious — giving CONSCIEN-TIOUS.

 

• Two points decide the question: the middle is -scien-, and the ending is -tious, never -cious or -teous.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Conscienteous — wrong; the ending has been written -teous on the analogy of 'courteous'.

 

• Option 2: Consciencious — wrong; the ending has been written -cious on the analogy of 'delicious'.

 

• Option 3: Conscentious — wrong; the i of -scien- has been dropped.

 

NOTE

 

• Distinguish the related words: conscience (the moral sense), conscious (awake and aware), conscientious (dutiful and thorough). All three are regularly confused in the exam.

question: Choose the correct one-word substitute for: 'A word or phrase that reads the same backwards as forwards'.
option_1: Anagram
option_2: Palindrome
option_3: Acronym
option_4: Pseudonym
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Palindrome.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A palindrome is a word, phrase or number that reads the same in both directions. (विलोमपद)
◦ Example: 'Malayalam', 'level' and 'madam' are palindromes.

 

• The word comes from Greek palin ('again, back') and dromos ('a running') — literally 'running back again'.

 

• All four options name kinds of wordplay or naming, so the answer turns on what exactly is done to the letters.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Anagram (वर्ण-विपर्यय): a word formed by rearranging the letters of another, as 'listen' and 'silent'.

 

• Option 3: Acronym (संक्षिप्ताक्षर शब्द): a word formed from the initial letters of several words, as 'NASA' or 'radar'.

 

• Option 4: Pseudonym (उपनाम, छद्म नाम): a false name adopted by an author in place of his own.

 

NOTE

 

• Complete the family for the exam: synonym (same meaning), antonym (opposite meaning), homonym (same form, different meaning), eponym (a person after whom something is named), toponym (a place name).

question: Choose the correct one-word substitute for: 'A statement accepted as true without proof, serving as the starting point of an argument'.
option_1: Hypothesis
option_2: Corollary
option_3: Axiom
option_4: Theorem
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Axiom.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• An axiom is a proposition assumed to be true without demonstration, from which other propositions are derived. (स्वयंसिद्ध सिद्धांत, अभिगृहीत)
◦ Example: The whole argument rests on the axiom that every citizen is equal before the law.

 

• The word comes from Greek axioma, 'that which is thought worthy or self-evident'.

 

• The decisive words in the definition are 'without proof' and 'starting point' — an axiom is where reasoning begins, not where it arrives.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Hypothesis (परिकल्पना): a provisional supposition put forward in order to be tested — it invites proof rather than dispensing with it.

 

• Option 2: Corollary (उपसिद्धांत): a proposition that follows immediately from one already proved.

 

• Option 4: Theorem (प्रमेय): a proposition that has been proved from axioms and earlier results.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the logical order in which these words stand: axiom (assumed) → theorem (proved from it) → corollary (following from the theorem); a hypothesis stands outside this chain, awaiting test.

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct option:

 

The auditors examined the accounts so _____ that not a single discrepancy escaped notice.
option_1: thorough
option_2: thoroughly
option_3: thoroughness
option_4: thoroughgoing
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. thoroughly.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The blank follows the action verb examined and describes how the examination was carried out. A word that modifies a verb in this way must be an adverb.

 

• Of the four forms offered, only thoroughly is an adverb. The structure is so + adverb + that, which introduces a clause of result:
◦ Example: He spoke so softly that nobody at the back could hear him.

 

• The completed sentence: The auditors examined the accounts so thoroughly that not a single discrepancy escaped notice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: thorough — the adjective; it would describe a noun, as in 'a thorough examination'.

 

• Option 3: thoroughness — the noun, which cannot follow 'so' in this structure.

 

• Option 4: thoroughgoing — another adjective, meaning complete or absolute, as in 'a thoroughgoing reform'.

 

NOTE

 

• Keep the two structures apart: so + adjective + that follows a linking verb — *He was so careful that ...*; so + adverb + that follows an action verb — *He worked so carefully that ...*

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The principal ordered for (1)/ two hundred additional copies (2)/ of the revised prospectus (3)/ before the admission season began. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. (1).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When order means 'to place an order for goods', it is used as a transitive verb and takes its object directly, without any preposition. 'Ordered for two hundred copies' is therefore wrong.

 

• Part (1) must read 'The principal ordered'. If a preposition is wanted, the noun must be used instead — *placed an order for two hundred copies*.

 

• The corrected sentence: The principal ordered two hundred additional copies of the revised prospectus before the admission season began.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (2) is correct — two hundred takes no plural -s when a number precedes it.

 

• Part (3) and Part (4) are sound; began correctly matches the past-time frame of the sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the contrast with the other sense of the verb: order somebody to do something does take a following structure — *The officer ordered the men to withdraw*. It is only the 'place an order' sense that must not take for.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The Ganga is (1)/ longest river (2)/ that flows through (3)/ the plains of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A superlative adjective must be preceded by the definite article the, because a superlative singles out one member from all the rest and is therefore definite by its very nature.

 

• Part (2) must read 'the longest river'.

 

• The corrected sentence: The Ganga is the longest river that flows through the plains of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — the names of rivers regularly take the in English: *the Ganga, the Nile, the Thames*.

 

• Part (3) and Part (4) are sound; the relative pronoun that properly introduces the defining clause.

 

NOTE

 

• Other places where the is obligatory: before superlatives (the best), before an ordinal (the first attempt), before a comparative used with 'of the two' (the taller of the two), and in the double comparative (the sooner, the better).

question:
Change the following from active to passive.

 

The villagers laughed at his warning.
option_1: His warning was laughed by the villagers.
option_2: His warning was being laughed at by the villagers.
option_3: His warning had been laughed at by the villagers.
option_4: His warning was laughed at by the villagers.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. His warning was laughed at by the villagers.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Laugh at is a prepositional verb: the verb and its preposition work as a single unit. When such a verb is made passive, the preposition must be retained immediately after the past participle.
◦ Active: They laughed at his warning. → Passive: His warning was laughed at.

 

• Steps applied here:
◦ The object of the preposition, his warning, becomes the subject.
◦ laughed at → was laughed at, the tense remaining the simple past.
◦ The villagers becomes the agent, introduced by the preposition by.

 

• The passive verb is therefore followed by two prepositions in succession — at by — which is correct and is the mark of this construction.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 drops the preposition at, leaving the verb without its necessary partner.

 

• Option 2 changes it to the past continuous.

 

• Option 3 changes the tense to the past perfect.

 

NOTE

 

• Other prepositional verbs that keep the preposition in the passive: look after, deal with, send for, listen to, rely on, account for, take care of. — *The patient was looked after by a trained nurse.*

question:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

The letters are sorted by the clerks every morning.
option_1: The clerks sorted the letters every morning.
option_2: The clerks have sorted the letters every morning.
option_3: The clerks are sorting the letters every morning.
option_4: The clerks sort the letters every morning.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The clerks sort the letters every morning.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the simple present passive — are sorted. Its active counterpart must also be in the simple present.

 

• Steps applied here:
◦ The agent the clerks becomes the subject.
◦ are sorted → sort.
◦ The letters becomes the object, and the by-phrase is dropped.

 

• The adverbial every morning marks a habitual action, which confirms that the simple present must be retained.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 shifts the sentence into the simple past.

 

• Option 2 gives the present perfect, reporting a completed action rather than a habit.

 

• Option 3 gives the present continuous, which cannot describe a settled routine introduced by 'every morning'.

 

NOTE

 

• Adverbials such as every day, always, usually, generally, often and never signal a habitual action and therefore call for the simple present.

question:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word.

 

The librarian placed the missing volume back on the shelf.
option_1: The second volume of the series has long been out of print.
option_2: He reached over and turned down the volume of the radio.
option_3: A leather-bound volume lay open on the reading desk.
option_4: The volume was catalogued under regional history.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. He reached over and turned down the volume of the radio.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word identical in spelling and pronunciation to another but carrying an entirely different meaning. (समनामी शब्द)

 

• In the given sentence volume means a single book, especially one of a set. The question therefore asks for the sentence in which the same word carries a different meaning.

 

• Option 2 uses volume to mean the loudness of a sound. The verb 'turned down' and the noun 'radio' fix this second sense beyond doubt.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1, Option 3 and Option 4 all use volume in the same bibliographical sense as the highlighted word, so none of them qualifies as a homonym.

 

• Volume has a third common sense — the amount of space a body occupies, as in 'the volume of a cylinder' — and a fourth in commerce, 'the volume of trade'.

 

NOTE

 

• Keep the three terms distinct: homonyms are alike in spelling and sound (volume, capital, pupil); homophones sound alike but are spelt differently (sight/site, principal/principle); homographs are spelt alike but may be pronounced differently (lead, tear, row).

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Her elder sister was married with a doctor from Pune last year.
option_1: married for
option_2: married by
option_3: married to
option_4: married against
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. married to.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb marry, in the passive, takes the preposition to before the person one is married to. The fixed pattern is be married to somebody. (विवाहित होना)
◦ Example: She has been married to him for twelve years.

 

• Married with is a common error in this position. With never introduces the spouse; it belongs to other patterns altogether — *married with the consent of both families* (attendant circumstance) and *married with two children* (that is, married and having two children).

 

• The corrected sentence: Her elder sister was married to a doctor from Pune last year.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: married for — for would suggest a motive, as in 'married for money', and does not fit here.

 

• Option 2: married by — by introduces the person who performs the ceremony, not the spouse: *They were married by the registrar*.

 

• Option 4: married against — no such collocation exists; against appears only in 'married against her wishes'.

 

NOTE

 

• Other relationship collocations frequently tested: engaged to, related to, attached to, devoted to, indebted to, but acquainted with and popular with.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Darkness used to be free. For almost the whole of human history the night sky was available to anybody who stepped outdoors, and the loss of it has been so gradual that most city dwellers do not know what is missing. A child born in a large Indian city today may reach adulthood without ever having seen the Milky Way, and will not feel deprived, because nothing announces the absence.

 

The cause is not the quantity of light we produce but the carelessness with which we aim it. A lamp designed to illuminate a road throws a good part of its output sideways and upwards, where it illuminates nothing at all and merely scatters in the atmosphere. This spilling of light beyond the area it was meant for is called light trespass, and it is the reason a single unshielded lamp can brighten the sky for a kilometre around it while leaving the pavement beneath it poorly lit.

 

The consequences are not confined to astronomy. Many insects navigate by the moon and are drawn instead to street lamps, where they circle until they die; the birds and bats that feed on them lose a food supply, and the plants those insects would have pollinated lose their pollinators. Migratory birds, which orient themselves by the stars, are disoriented by illuminated towers. An ecological chain that took a long time to assemble is disturbed by an object nobody thinks of as a pollutant.

 

What makes the problem unusual is that the remedy is immediate and cheap. A shield fitted over a lamp so that its light falls only downwards costs very little, saves the electricity that was being thrown at the sky, and improves visibility on the ground at the same time. Almost no other environmental problem offers a correction that pays for itself within a year.

 

Yet the sky continues to brighten, and the reason is that nobody owns it. A polluted river has residents along its bank who will complain; a lost horizon has no constituency. Until the night is treated as a shared resource rather than as empty space above private property, the remedy will remain available and unused.

 

What does the author identify as the main cause of the loss of the night sky?
option_1: The carelessness with which light is aimed rather than the amount produced.
option_2: The sheer quantity of light that cities now produce.
option_3: The growth of the population in large Indian cities.
option_4: The replacement of older lamps by brighter modern ones.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The carelessness with which light is aimed rather than the amount produced.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states it directly at the head of the second paragraph: 'The cause is not the quantity of light we produce but the carelessness with which we aim it.'

 

• The illustration follows immediately: a road lamp 'throws a good part of its output sideways and upwards, where it illuminates nothing at all and merely scatters in the atmosphere.'

 

• The construction 'not A but B' places the whole weight on B, and the question asks for exactly that.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 is the very explanation the passage rejects in its opening clause.

 

• Option 3 introduces population growth, which the passage never mentions.

 

• Option 4 blames the brightness of modern lamps, whereas the passage blames their direction.

 

NOTE

 

• Watch the pattern 'not A but B': the correct option restates B, while A is almost always offered as a distractor.

Until the night is treated as a shared resource rather than as empty space above private property, the remedy will remain available and unused.

 

What does the term 'light trespass' mean as used in the passage?
option_1: The spilling of light beyond the area it was meant to serve.
option_2: The theft of electricity from street-lighting cables.
option_3: The legal right of a neighbour to object to a bright lamp.
option_4: The dimming of a lamp as its bulb grows old.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The spilling of light beyond the area it was meant to serve.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage defines the term in the sentence in which it appears: 'This spilling of light beyond the area it was meant for is called light trespass.'

 

• Its effect is then described: a single unshielded lamp 'can brighten the sky for a kilometre around it while leaving the pavement beneath it poorly lit.'

 

• The word trespass is used figuratively — the light goes where it has no business to go — and not in any legal or criminal sense.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 reads 'trespass' as theft and misses the figurative use.

 

• Option 3 reads it as a legal right, which the passage nowhere confers.

 

• Option 4 describes a failing bulb, a matter the passage does not raise.

 

NOTE

 

• When a passage supplies a definition in the very sentence that introduces a technical term — usually with 'is called' or 'that is' — the correct option is a paraphrase of that definition.

Yet the sky continues to brighten, and the reason is that nobody owns it. A polluted river has residents along its bank who will complain; a lost horizon has no constituency. Until the night is treated as a shared resource rather than as empty space above private property, the remedy will remain available and unused.

 

According to the passage, what happens to insects that are drawn to street lamps?
option_1: They pollinate the plants growing beside the road.
option_2: They navigate more accurately than they would by moonlight.
option_3: They circle the lamps until they die, and the creatures that feed on them lose a food supply.
option_4: They migrate to darker areas outside the city.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. They circle the lamps until they die, and the creatures that feed on them lose a food supply.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states that many insects 'navigate by the moon and are drawn instead to street lamps, where they circle until they die.'

 

• The consequence runs down the chain: 'the birds and bats that feed on them lose a food supply, and the plants those insects would have pollinated lose their pollinators.'

 

• The author's summing-up is that 'an ecological chain that took a long time to assemble is disturbed by an object nobody thinks of as a pollutant.'

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reverses the passage: the point is precisely that the pollination does not happen.

 

• Option 2 contradicts the text, which says the insects are drawn away from their natural guide.

 

• Option 4 describes a migration the passage does not mention.

 

NOTE

 

• Where a passage traces a chain of consequences, the correct option usually reproduces more than one link of that chain; options that stop at the first link are often incomplete.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Darkness used to be free. For almost the whole of human history the night sky was available to anybody who stepped outdoors, and the loss of it has been so gradual that most city dwellers do not know what is missing. A child born in a large Indian city today may reach adulthood without ever having seen the Milky Way, and will not feel deprived, because nothing announces the absence.

 

The cause is not the quantity of light we produce but the carelessness with which we aim it. A lamp designed to illuminate a road throws a good part of its output sideways and upwards, where it illuminates nothing at all and merely scatters in the atmosphere. This spilling of light beyond the area it was meant for is called light trespass, and it is the reason a single unshielded lamp can brighten the sky for a kilometre around it while leaving the pavement beneath it poorly lit.

 

The consequences are not confined to astronomy. Many insects navigate by the moon and are drawn instead to street lamps, where they circle until they die; the birds and bats that feed on them lose a food supply, and the plants those insects would have pollinated lose their pollinators. Migratory birds, which orient themselves by the stars, are disoriented by illuminated towers. An ecological chain that took a long time to assemble is disturbed by an object nobody thinks of as a pollutant.

 

What makes the problem unusual is that the remedy is immediate and cheap. A shield fitted over a lamp so that its light falls only downwards costs very little, saves the electricity that was being thrown at the sky, and improves visibility on the ground at the same time. Almost no other environmental problem offers a correction that pays for itself within a year.

 

Yet the sky continues to brighten, and the reason is that nobody owns it. A polluted river has residents along its bank who will complain; a lost horizon has no constituency. Until the night is treated as a shared resource rather than as empty space above private property, the remedy will remain available and unused.

 

Why does the author describe the fitting of a shield over a lamp?
option_1: To argue that street lighting should be switched off at midnight.
option_2: To show that the remedy is cheap, saves electricity and improves visibility at the same time.
option_3: To explain why modern lamps are more expensive than older ones.
option_4: To suggest that astronomers should be consulted before roads are lit.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To show that the remedy is cheap, saves electricity and improves visibility at the same time.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The shield is introduced to support the claim that opens the paragraph: 'What makes the problem unusual is that the remedy is immediate and cheap.'

 

• The passage then lists the three benefits together: a shield 'costs very little, saves the electricity that was being thrown at the sky, and improves visibility on the ground at the same time.'

 

• The author adds the comparison that gives the example its force: 'Almost no other environmental problem offers a correction that pays for itself within a year.'

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 proposes switching lights off, which the passage never recommends — its remedy is to aim them properly.

 

• Option 3 concerns the cost of lamps, a comparison the passage does not make.

 

• Option 4 brings in astronomers, whereas the passage says expressly that the consequences are 'not confined to astronomy'.

 

NOTE

 

• 'Why does the author describe X' questions ask for the function of an example. Find the claim the paragraph opens with; the correct option will show X supporting that claim.

According to the author, why does the sky continue to brighten despite an easy remedy?
option_1: Because the shields required are not manufactured in sufficient numbers.
option_2: Because electricity is too cheap for anyone to bother saving it.
option_3: Because most people prefer a brightly lit street to a dark one.
option_4: Because nobody owns the sky, so its loss has no constituency to defend it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Because nobody owns the sky, so its loss has no constituency to defend it.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The final paragraph gives the reason plainly: 'Yet the sky continues to brighten, and the reason is that nobody owns it.'

 

• The contrast that follows makes the point concrete: 'A polluted river has residents along its bank who will complain; a lost horizon has no constituency.'

 

• The author's closing condition follows from it: until the night is treated as 'a shared resource rather than as empty space above private property', the remedy will remain 'available and unused'.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 invents a shortage of shields that the passage does not mention.

 

• Option 2 contradicts the passage, which counts the saved electricity among the benefits.

 

• Option 3 attributes a preference to the public that the passage never records; indeed it notes that an unshielded lamp leaves the pavement poorly lit.

 

NOTE

 

• The last paragraph of an argumentative passage usually carries both the reason and the condition for change; comprehension items on 'why does it persist' are almost always answered there.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

She said, “I am writing a letter to my aunt.”
option_1: She said that she is writing a letter to her aunt.
option_2: She said that she had written a letter to her aunt.
option_3: She said that she was writing a letter to her aunt.
option_4: She said that she wrote a letter to her aunt.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. She said that she was writing a letter to her aunt.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported words are in the present continuous (am writing). After the past reporting verb said, this backshifts to the past continuous:
◦ is/am/are + V-ing → was/were + V-ing

 

• The pronouns shift with the speaker: I becomes she, and my becomes her.

 

• The conjunction that is supplied and the inverted commas are removed. The completed sentence: She said that she was writing a letter to her aunt.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 leaves the tense unchanged, so no backshift has taken place.

 

• Option 2 uses the past perfect, which corresponds to the direct form 'I had written' and reports a completed action.

 

• Option 4 uses the simple past, losing the sense of an action in progress at the moment of speaking.

 

NOTE

 

• The full backshift table: simple present → simple past; present continuous → past continuous; present perfect → past perfect; simple past → past perfect; past continuous → past perfect continuous. The past perfect itself does not change further.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

He said to the examiner, “Let me try the last question once more.”
option_1: He told the examiner to try the last question once more.
option_2: He asked the examiner whether he tried the last question once more.
option_3: He said to the examiner that let him try the last question once more.
option_4: He requested the examiner that he might be allowed to try the last question once more.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. He requested the examiner that he might be allowed to try the last question once more.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• 'Let me ...' addressed to another person expresses a request for permission, not a suggestion. In indirect speech it is reported with requested and the structure that + subject + might be allowed to + verb.
◦ Example: He said to the guard, 'Let me go.' → He requested the guard that he might be allowed to go.

 

• Note the difference from 'Let us ...', which proposes joint action and is reported with suggested that ... should.

 

• The pronoun me becomes he, since the speaker is being reported.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 makes the examiner the person who is to try the question, reversing who was to do the trying.

 

• Option 2 turns a request for permission into a question about the past.

 

• Option 3 keeps the word let inside a that-clause, which reported speech does not permit.

 

NOTE

 

• Summary of the three 'let' patterns: 'Let me/him ...' (permission) → *requested that ... might be allowed to*; 'Let us ...' (proposal) → *suggested that ... should*; 'Let the door be closed' (passive imperative) → *ordered that the door should be closed*.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

He said that he wished he had listened to his father's advice.
option_1: “I wish I had listened to my father's advice,” he said.
option_2: “I wish I listened to my father's advice,” he said.
option_3: “I wished I had listened to his father's advice,” he said.
option_4: “I wish I would have listened to my father's advice,” he said.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. “I wish I had listened to my father's advice,” he said.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported clause 'he wished he had listened' shows a regret about the past. In direct speech the pattern is 'I wish + past perfect', which is the fixed form for regretting something that did not happen.
◦ Example: I wish I had taken the earlier train.

 

• Two changes are needed: the backshifted reporting verb wished reverts to the present wish, and the pronouns he and his revert to I and my.

 

• The past perfect (had listened) is retained, because it belongs to the 'wish' structure itself and is not a product of backshift.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 uses the simple past listened, which would express a wish about the present, not a regret about the past.

 

• Option 3 keeps the past wished and the third-person his, both of which belong to the indirect version.

 

• Option 4 uses would have listened, which is not admitted after 'wish'.

 

NOTE

 

• The three 'wish' patterns are worth memorising: wish + past simple for a present regret (*I wish I knew*); wish + past perfect for a past regret (*I wish I had known*); wish + would for irritation at a habit (*I wish he would stop*).

question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:

 

1. These range from the thickness of the wire to the temperature of the room.
2. The resistance of a conductor is not a fixed quantity.
3. Engineers therefore specify the conditions under which a stated rating holds.
4. It varies with several measurable conditions.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. 2-4-1-3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sentence 2 opens the paragraph: it names the subject — the resistance of a conductor — and makes the general negative claim about it.

 

• Sentence 4 follows, because the pronoun 'It' refers back to that resistance, and because the phrase 'several measurable conditions' announces a list.

 

• Sentence 1 supplies the list, and its opening word 'These' points back to the conditions just announced in sentence 4.

 

• Sentence 3 concludes, marked by 'therefore', drawing the practical consequence for engineers.

 

• The chain is therefore claim → what it depends on → the items → practical consequence: 2-4-1-3.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (4-2-1-3) opens with the pronoun 'It', which has no antecedent.

 

• Option 3 (2-1-4-3) places 'These' before the conditions have been announced.

 

• Option 4 (1-2-4-3) likewise begins with an unattached demonstrative.

 

NOTE

 

• Two cues settle this question type at once: a pronoun cannot precede the noun it stands for, and a sentence announcing a number — 'several conditions', 'two methods' — must come before the list it promises.

question:
Rearrange the following sentences in correct order to make a logical passage.

 

1. The clay is then shaped on a wheel and left to dry slowly in the shade.
2. Terracotta begins with ordinary river clay, cleaned of grit and stones.
3. Only after drying is the piece fired, which fixes its familiar red colour.
4. A vessel made in this way will hold water for a generation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. 2-1-3-4.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sentence 2 opens the paragraph: it names the subject and states the first step. The verb 'begins' settles its position beyond argument.

 

• Sentence 1 follows, marked by 'then' and by 'The clay', which refers back to the river clay of sentence 2.

 

• Sentence 3 comes next, since 'Only after drying' presupposes the drying described at the end of sentence 1.

 

• Sentence 4 closes with the result — a vessel that will last a generation.

 

• The order is therefore material → shaping and drying → firing → result: 2-1-3-4.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (1-2-3-4) opens with 'The clay' before any clay has been introduced.

 

• Option 3 (2-3-1-4) places the firing before the shaping and drying that must precede it.

 

• Option 4 (3-2-1-4) begins in the middle of the process altogether.

 

NOTE

 

• In process passages, follow the chain of definite articles and time words: 'begins' marks the opening, 'then' and 'only after' fix the middle, and the finished product closes the paragraph.
